content: Central diatoms, also referred to as Centrales, represent a traditional subgroup of the heterokont algae known as diatoms. The name of this order is derived from the characteristic shape of their cell walls, also called valves or frustules, which are typically circular or ellipsoid when viewed from the valve perspective. These valves often exhibit radially symmetrical ornamental patterns, which, under an optical microscope, may appear as dots. Additionally, some central diatoms possess spines on their valves. These spines can serve to increase the cell's surface area, thereby reducing its sinking rate, or act as a deterrent against zooplankton grazers. Unlike pennate diatoms, central diatoms lack a raphe, a slit-like structure used for motility in other diatom groups. Regarding their cell cycle, the vegetative cells of central diatoms are diploid and undergo mitosis during normal cell division. In species that reproduce sexually, oogamous meiosis occurs, resulting in the production of haploid gametes, which may be either ova or sperm cells. These gametes fuse to form a zygote, which subsequently enlarges to develop into an auxospore. The auxospore then gives rise to full-sized vegetative cells. In certain taxonomic classifications, central diatoms are alternatively referred to as the Order Coscinodiscophyceae.
